content: Zinc sulfate is a parenteral trace mineral approved by the FDA for the prevention of zinc deficiency. Common side effects include indigestion, nausea, and vomiting. For adults, zinc sulfate injection is used as a supplement to intravenous solutions in total parenteral nutrition (TPN) to maintain plasma zinc levels and prevent depletion of endogenous stores. The standard dosage is 5 to 4 mg of zinc per day, with an additional 2 mg per day recommended in acute catabolic states. For patients with significant stool or ileostomy output, 1 mg of zinc per kilogram of output is advised. Frequent monitoring of zinc blood levels is recommended for patients receiving higher-than-usual maintenance doses. For pediatric patients, the recommended dosage for full-term infants and children up to 5 years of age is 100 mcg of zinc per kilogram per day. For premature infants weighing less than 1500 grams and up to 3 kilograms in body weight, 300 mcg of zinc per kilogram per day is suggested. Zinc sulfate injection should be added aseptically to TPN solutions under a laminar flow hood. Zinc is physically compatible with the electrolytes and vitamins typically present in amino acid/dextrose solutions used for TPN. Parenteral drug products should be visually inspected for particulate matter and discoloration whenever the solution and container permit. There is limited information regarding off-label uses, contraindications, warnings, clinical trial experiences, postmarketing experiences, and drug interactions for zinc sulfate. Additionally, there is no FDA guidance on its use in specific populations, including pregnant women, nursing mothers, pediatric patients, geriatric patients, or immunocompromised individuals. Symptoms of zinc overdose from oral ingestion of large amounts (30–44 grams) have resulted in death. Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, dizziness, abdominal pain, lethargy, and incoordination. Single intravenous doses of 1 to 2 mg of zinc per kilogram of body weight have been administered to adult leukemia patients without toxic effects. Normal plasma zinc levels range from approximately 88 to 112 mcg/100 mL, but plasma levels sufficient to cause toxicity in humans are not well established. Calcium supplements may provide a protective effect against zinc toxicity. Zinc acts as a cofactor for over 70 enzymes, including alkaline phosphatase, lactic dehydrogenase, and RNA/DNA polymerase. It facilitates wound healing, supports normal growth rates, maintains skin hydration, and preserves the senses of taste and smell. Zinc supplementation during TPN prevents deficiency symptoms such as parakeratosis, hypogeusia, anorexia, dysosmia, geophagia, hypogonadism, growth retardation, and hepatosplenomegaly. Plasma zinc levels below 20 mcg/100 mL have been associated with dermatitis and alopecia in TPN patients. Zinc sulfate injection is a sterile, non-pyrogenic solution intended for use as an additive to TPN solutions. The pH is adjusted with sulfuric acid, and the solution contains no preservatives. Any unused portion should be discarded. There is limited information on the pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, and nonclinical toxicology of zinc sulfate. Clinical studies on zinc sulfate are also limited. Zinc sulfate injection is supplied as a 1 mg/mL solution in 10 mL single-dose vials. It should be stored at 20°C to 25°C (68°F to 77°F), with excursions permitted between 15°C and 30°C (59°F to 86°F). There is no established interaction between alcohol and zinc sulfate. Patients should consult their healthcare provider regarding the effects of alcohol consumption while taking this medication. Brand names for zinc sulfate include M2 Zinc 50 and Zn Plus Protein.
